query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, nearly equiatomic addition of aluminum into the FeCoNi alloy (i.e. preparing an equiatomic FeCoNiAl high‐entropy alloy) will drive partial ordering and/or a phase transformation (e.g. formation of B2‐ordered nano‐precipitates within the dominant FCC matrix) that increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy and enhances domain wall pinning, thereby increasing the coercivity relative to the baseline soft ferromagnetic FeCoNi derivatives (such as FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt).
generation.material_initial_state: An FCC-structured, soft ferromagnetic, equiatomic FeCoNi alloy with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Substitute a fraction of the Fe, Co, and Ni uniformly with Al to achieve a near equiatomic multicomponent FeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy while preserving high configurational entropy (≥1.0R).
generation.conditions: Arc-melted and homogenized equiatomic alloy processed under conditions that promote a uniform microstructure; the intervention is expected to be effective when the addition of Al is sufficient to trigger partial ordering (e.g. B2 precipitate formation) but not so large as to completely transform the structure or suppress ferromagnetism.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanometer-scale, coherently embedded ordered (B2) precipitates within the dominant FCC matrix, which serve as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
generation.mechanism: The Al addition creates local lattice distortions and drives partial chemical ordering. This ordering increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy and introduces heterogeneity in exchange interactions, resulting in enhanced domain wall pinning. The interplay between the soft FCC matrix and the harder, ordered regions increases the resistance to magnetization reversal and thus elevates coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a significantly increased coercive field compared to prior soft derivatives (FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt), while largely maintaining high saturation magnetization. The magnitude of the increase is uncertain but should be detectable by standard magnetic hysteresis measurements.
generation.baseline: Prior FeCoNi-based HEAs (e.g., those with Pd or Pt) that remain single-phase FCC with soft ferromagnetism and low coercive fields.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected only when the Al addition is within a narrow compositional window (close to equiatomic ratios) that maintains high configurational entropy; excessive Al may cause a complete structural transformation or degrade magnetic saturation. Additionally, processing factors (e.g. cooling rate, annealing conditions) that influence the degree and scale of ordering will affect the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by the notion that induced ordering in HEAs can enhance coercivity through increased anisotropy and domain wall pinning, the exact quantitative improvement and optimal Al concentration remain to be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize an equiatomic FeCoNiAl alloy using arc-melting and homogenization to obtain a uniform microstructure. Prepare a reference sample of FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt with previously reported soft properties. Use X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to characterize the phases and detect evidence of partial ordering (e.g. B2-precipitates). Measure the hysteresis loops using vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) at room temperature.
measurements: XRD patterns to identify phase structure and detect any ordering peaks indicative of B2 formation
TEM/SEM micrographs to visualize nanoscale precipitates
Magnetic hysteresis loops to extract coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiAl alloy does not exhibit any detectable increase in coercivity relative to the baseline FeCoNi derivative (i.e. coercivity remains similar or lower) or if there is no evidence of induced ordering (e.g. B2 phase formation) in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.
